label: Making friends
rationale: Meeting someone new: making friends, becoming friends with one person, swapping names, going up to someone, and chances to meet people.
mixUps: tomodachi ga dekiru is gaining friends in general (tomodachi dekita), while one person is X to tomodachi ni naru; neither is tomodachi o tsukuru. 'Tell me your name' is namae oshiete, not iu, and going up to someone is koe o kakeru, not hanasu.

targets.verbSense: come into being, be made; also 'can do' and 'be ready'
targets.trap: English 'make' leads to tomodachi o tsukuru, which natives use for setting out to make friends (tomodachi tsukuritai); 'I've made a friend' is tomodachi dekita.
partners: kodomo (child: kodomo dekita = we're expecting; akachan works too)
targets.use: Said once a friendship has formed, so mostly in the past: tomodachi dekita (I've made a friend). kareshi / kanojo dekita (got a boyfriend / girlfriend) works the same way.
targets.notes: Wanting friends is usually tomodachi hoshii or tomodachi tsukuritai. Having them takes ga iru, as in kodomo ga iru: dekita is the moment it happens, iru is having them (tomodachi iru?). Becoming friends with one person is X to tomodachi ni naru.

example.ja: こっちでもう友達できた？

examplePolite.romaji: kochira de tomodachi wa dekimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: こちらで友達はできましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you made any friends here?

targets.trap: English 'make friends with him' leads to tomodachi o tsukuru, which is setting out to make friends in general (tomodachi tsukuritai). With a particular person it's kare to tomodachi ni natta, and 'I've made a friend' is tomodachi dekita.
partners: koibito (a couple; tsukiau is the usual 'start going out')
targets.use: Takes to for the other person: kare to tomodachi ni natta (I became friends with him). Mostly told in the past, about where or how a friendship started.
targets.notes: nakayoku naru (get close) is the near twin: sugu nakayoku natta (we hit it off right away). tomodachi ni narou = let's be friends.

example.romaji: kanojo to wa daigaku de tomodachi ni natta.
example.ja: 彼女とは大学で友達になった。
example.english: She and I became friends at uni.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo to wa daigaku de tomodachi ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女とは大学で友達になりました。
examplePolite.english: She and I became friends at university.

targets.verbSense: teach; also tell, let someone know (information)
targets.trap: English 'tell me your name' leads to iu, and namae o iu is real Japanese: it's saying a name out loud (in a roll call, or saying your own). Asking someone to share their name, number or the way takes oshieru: namae oshiete.
partners: michi (the way: michi o oshieru = give directions)
targets.use: Mostly the request namae oshiete (what's your name?), a friendly alternative to onamae wa? or namae nante iu no?. The same oshieru asks for any personal details: bangou oshiete (give me your number).
targets.notes: onamae wa? is the plain polite question (at a counter, or to a child); between friends namae nante iu no? is common.

example.ja: よかったら、名前教えてくれる？
example.english: If you don't mind, what's your name?

examplePolite.romaji: yokattara, onamae o oshiete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、お名前を教えてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Would you mind telling me your name?

targets.english: speak to, call out to; ask along
targets.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; here, direct your voice at someone
targets.trap: 'Talk to someone' leads to hanasu, which is fine once you're talking: X to hanasu is chatting with X, X ni hanasu is telling X something. Going up to someone, calling them over or giving them a shout is koe o kakeru (hanashikakeru also works for starting a chat).
partners: kotoba (words: yasashii kotoba o kakeru = say something kind to someone)
targets.use: Used for going up to someone, or asking to be told: nanka attara koe kakete (give me a shout if anything comes up). Also the everyday way to invite someone along: tanaka-san ni mo koe kakeyou ka? (shall we ask Tanaka too?). koe kakerareta can mean someone came up to you, including being hit on.
targets.notes: hanashikakeru (start talking to someone) is the close single verb. Same kakeru as denwa o kakeru (make a call) and meiwaku o kakeru, in a different sense.

example.ja: なんかあったら声かけてね。
example.english: Give me a shout if you need anything.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika attara koe o kakete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 何かあったら声をかけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please let me know if you need anything.

targets.trap: English 'I never meet anyone' leads to dare ni mo awanai, which sounds like you never see people at all. Meeting someone new is talked about as a deai (an encounter): deai ga nai.
targets.use: Mostly in the negative, the stock complaint deai ga nai (I never meet anyone), and in good wishes: ii deai ga arimasu you ni (hope you meet someone great). Often about romance, but it also covers new friends at a new job or school.
targets.notes: deau is the verb, for meeting for the first time or by chance: daigaku de deatta (we met at uni).

example.romaji: shokuba ni zenzen deai nai n da yo.
example.ja: 職場に全然出会いないんだよ。
example.english: I never meet anyone at work.

examplePolite.romaji: shokuba ni wa zenzen deai ga nai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 職場には全然出会いがないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: I never get to meet anyone at work.

reviewPool.english: be capable, good at one's job
have good taste, a good eye
go out for fun; go visit
